Subject: Network Safelist and Egress Modes for On-Prem Redwood Private Endpoint

Hi team,

Thanks for the runbook call earlier — following up with a consolidated note and two attachments (safelist-ip-table.csv, proposal-egress-modes.pdf) to make the firewall and egress decision easier for your on-prem/private deployment. High-level asks:

- Confirm which egress mode you prefer (see options below).
- Confirm static egress IP/NAT ranges if you want customer-controlled egress.
- Confirm whether TLS inspection / MITM is in scope (this impacts mTLS requirements).

Executive summary (short):
- Redwood Private will attempt to work in three deployment modes: 1) Managed Relay (Redwood egress IPs, mutual TLS), 2) Customer NAT (all outbound flows originate from your fixed NAT/public IPs), 3) Strict Offline (no external outbound; synchronous ops degraded).
- Attachment safelist-ip-table.csv lists exact ports, hostnames, and short justifications we usually need for the Managed Relay and hybrid modes.

Key technical notes (quick):
- Required outbound destinations (DNS, package repos, telemetry, auth): see CSV. We try to minimize dependencies — most flows are outbound HTTPS to well-known hostnames.
- Inbound to the on-prem endpoint is not required for normal inference traffic — requests are proxied out. However, if you want webhooks or callback URLs, those are inbound and must be configured separately.
- Prefer deny-by-default firewall policy with explicit allow entries for the entries in the attachment.

Proposed next step: 30-min sync next week to pick an egress mode and finalize static IPs.

Regards,
Aditya
Aditya Rao
Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

Attachment stubs: safelist-ip-table.csv (CSV with hosts/ips/ports), proposal-egress-modes.pdf (short description + diagrams)

Aditya — thanks for this. A few clarifying questions from our side before we lock a mode: 

1) TLS inspection: we have an outbound TLS inspection appliance. If you require mTLS client auth from the appliance's IP, we need to confirm who terminates TLS where. Does Redwood support connecting through a TLS-inspecting proxy while preserving client certs?

2) Outbound IPs: if you ask us to use Customer NAT mode, can you provide a short list of required destination IPs so our NAT preserve rules can be created? We prefer not to open large CIDR blocks.

3) Logging & audit: we need to ensure request/response metadata is logged for SOC-2 audits and retained per our policy. If using Managed Relay, can Redwood provide access to syslog or a webhook export?

Preference: we prefer Customer NAT (avoid third-party egress) but will evaluate Managed Relay if it reduces complexity.

Samir — thanks for the quick turnaround. Answers and an implementation proposal below. I pasted the key excerpts here and attached the CSV/PDF for copy/paste.

Short answers first:
- TLS inspection: Redwood supports proxying through TLS-inspecting middleboxes but requires either 1) passthrough of end-to-end mTLS (preferred) or 2) a trusted proxy with a customer-managed client cert that Redwood can validate. If inspection terminates TLS and re-encrypts, we need the proxy to present a client cert we accept or operate in Customer NAT mode.
- Destination IPs: For Customer NAT mode we only require DNS hostnames (we publish A/AAAA records) and a small set of IPs for fallback; full list in safelist-ip-table.csv. If you require strict IP-only rules, use the CSV's ip column and accept that IPs may change; we recommend FQDN-based allow rules when possible.
- Logging & audit: Managed Relay can export request headers + token metadata to a webhook or SIEM (syslog/CEF) — we can run a 30-day retention by config. Customer NAT mode requires you to forward your local logs to your SIEM; Redwood will provide an audit-webhook for server-side events if you enable the integration.

Detailed policy & recommended rules (example iptables / firewall snippets):

- Baseline policy (recommended):
  - Default: DROP
  - Allow: Established,Related
  - Allow: DNS -> your resolver (UDP/TCP 53)
  - Allow: outbound to destination hostnames in safelist (HTTPS/443)
  - Allow: NTP to internal NTP servers or trusted pool (UDP/123)

Example iptables (customer NAT mode, simplify for review):
  iptables -P INPUT DROP
  iptables -A INPUT -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT
  iptables -A OUTPUT -p udp --dport 53 -d 10.0.0.2 -j ACCEPT  # your DNS resolver
  iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -d 34.123.45.67 -j ACCEPT  # redwood relay fallback IP

Egress modes (concise):
- Managed Relay (Redwood egress): Redwood accepts encrypted egress from customer endpoint and routes via Redwood relay pool. Pros: minimal NAT config, centralized logs + telemetry, simpler on-prem setup. Cons: customer outbound to Redwood egress IPs.
- Customer NAT (preferred by many regulated customers): All outbound originates from your NAT; Redwood lists required hostnames/IPs for firewall rules. Pros: full control over egress, easier compliance. Cons: requires you to publish stable NAT IPs and possibly open DNS/OCSP endpoints.
- Strict Offline (air-gapped / limited): No external outbound. Only offline model bundles allowed, periodic manual syncs. Pros: maximum data control. Cons: many features disabled (telemetry, auto-updates).

Hostname vs IP guidance: put hostname allow rules where possible (e.g., proxies that support SNI allow-lists). If your firewall only supports IPs, we can provide an "IP snapshot" CSV but recommend a weekly syncing process (we publish a signed manifest).

Fallbacks & graceful degradation: if Managed Relay is chosen and the relay is unreachable, Redwood can fall back to local inference mode (if configured with model bundle). We recommend a canary window on rollout.

Attachments referenced: safelist-ip-table.csv (column: service, hostname, ip_snapshot, ports, purpose), proposal-egress-modes.pdf (diagram + mutual action plan).

Proposed timeline (if you choose Customer NAT):
- Day 0: Confirm NAT IPs + approve CSV
- Day 1-2: Firewall rules staged in lab
- Day 3: Plan cutover & smoke test
- Day 5: Production cutover

Let me know if you want me to produce an iptables-format file for your ops team to drop in.

—Aditya
